title: Arrow prayers (Nehemiah 2:4)
hook: before the king answers, Nehemiah fires a silent prayer upward

segments.voice: Yesterday, the examen: Ignatius's nightly look back over the day. Your line was where was he today? Today, a prayer that takes about one second.

Someone important turns to you and says: so, what do you want? The interview. The doctor. The boss with one minute between meetings. Your mouth is open, and there's no time to think. The same question once came in the Persian court, about four and a half centuries before Jesus. A Jewish man named Nehemiah is cupbearer to King Artaxerxes: he serves the king's wine. He's just heard that the walls of Jerusalem are rubble, and he can't hide his grief. The king notices his sad face, and the text says, "Then I was very sore afraid." A sad servant in front of a king was a risk. Then the king asks the question. What do you want? Nehemiah has maybe a second.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU WANT?` → `A CUPBEARER TO A KING.` → `ONE SECOND TO ANSWER.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse, in the King James Bible: "Then the king said unto me, For what dost thou make request? So I prayed to the God of heaven." And in the very next breath, he answers the king. No words recorded, no kneeling, no closed eyes. Between the question and the answer, a prayer went up, and nobody in the room saw it. Christians came to call this an arrow prayer: short, silent, fired upward in the middle of life. Augustine wrote of monks in the Egyptian desert, the same desert as the Jesus Prayer, who prayed all day in quick, brief bursts. But the arrow didn't come from nowhere. In chapter one, when the bad news first came, Nehemiah sat down and wept, and fasted and prayed for days. Months passed before the king ever asked. So the arrow flew from a bow that had been strung for a long time. The long prayer and the short one belong together. The Bible is full of these arrows. A mother pleading for her daughter, in Matthew: "Lord, help me." Peter, sinking into the waves: "Lord, save me." Three words each. Catholics, Orthodox Christians and Protestants all have their short prayers for the middle of things. For Nehemiah, it worked: the king said yes, and he went home to rebuild the wall.
screen: `A PRAYER BETWEEN QUESTION AND ANSWER.` · `THE BOW WAS STRUNG FOR MONTHS.` · `LORD, HELP ME. LORD, SAVE ME.` · then, large: `SHORT PRAYERS FLY.`

segments.voice: Think of the next conversation you'll have today, with a coworker, a child, a cashier, someone on the phone, and picture the moment before the first word. If you pray, send up a short line in three seconds, like the mother's "Lord, help me," or a few words of your own; if you don't, take one slow breath and wish them well. Then let the rest of the time be quiet.
Arrow prayers. Short, silent prayers sent up in the middle of life, like Nehemiah's before the king. Today's word.
Your line: short prayers fly. Nobody in the room has to know. That's one hundred three.

howItsDone: Many Christians pray short, silent prayers through the day, before a meeting, at a siren, in a moment of fear, alongside longer times of prayer; Orthodox Christians often use the Jesus Prayer this way.

trapdoor: what you thought: prayer needs time, a quiet room and closed eyes.
what it means: Nehemiah prays in the one second between a king's question and his answer, and nobody sees it.
what a scholar hears: a cupbearer served the Persian king's wine, a post of close trust; a servant looking sad before the king was a real risk, which is why he was afraid.

notes: Date: Nehemiah's request to Artaxerxes (I) is usually placed around 445 BCE, 'about four and a half centuries before Jesus'. Confirm.
'Months passed': Nehemiah 1:1 is in Chisleu and 2:1 in Nisan, roughly four months apart. Confirm.
Cupbearer tasting the king's wine first is a common description of the office; the text itself only says he was the king's cupbearer (1:11) and served wine (2:1). Confirm the phrasing.
'Arrow prayer' as a Christian term and the link to the Egyptian desert monks follows Augustine's Letter 130, which describes brief prayers 'darted' quickly; paraphrased, not quoted. Confirm.
Reading of 'Pray without ceasing' as keeping a door open all day is presented as how many Christians hear it; confirm it is fair across traditions.
